strengths: The paper presents a coherent and well-motivated framework (DeGSS) that unifies geometry, appearance, and kinematics of articulated objects in a single deformable Gaussian field, addressing a real limitation of prior two-state, single-part pipelines.

The progressive coarse-to-fine part segmentation (trajectory-based clustering + visibility-guided SAM prompting + boundary-aware Gaussian splitting) is a sensible and technically detailed mechanism for automatic part discovery without predefined part counts.

Strong empirical evaluation: an enlarged PartNet-Mobility split with two- and three-part objects, comprehensive comparisons against PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, and ArtGS with consistent improvements across joint and Chamfer metrics, plus reasonable ablations (refinement stage, number of interaction states K).

The RS-Art dataset (18 real objects, 6 categories, multi-state RGB-D captures paired with reverse-engineered URDF/USD digital twins) is a valuable community resource that addresses the scarcity of real-world articulated-object benchmarks.

The ability to interpolate latent codes and control individual parts (Fig. 3, Fig. 12) demonstrates a genuine capability gap relative to prior two-state methods, and the limitations section is candid and well-written.
weaknesses: The 'fully self-supervised' claim is overstated: the method relies on a VLM (InstructBLIP) to estimate the part count and on SAM for mask-guided splitting, so it depends on large pretrained foundation models and heuristic thresholds (tau_mot, tau_vis, 2% cluster pruning, r < 0.05 for joint typing). No ablation quantifies the robustness of the VLM-based part-count estimation, a critical component of the pipeline.

Evaluation protocol concerns: results are reported from a 'first run' with acknowledged large run-to-run variance in baselines, but no mean/std over multiple runs is given for any method; several baseline entries carry '*' failure marks, and how failures are scored/aggregated is not precisely defined.

Real-data evaluation is thin: only ArtGS is compared on RS-Art (Table 4), the main-paper Section 5.4 is qualitative only, and the quantitative real results are relegated to the appendix; a broader comparison or at least additional baselines on real data would be needed to support the claim of real-world robustness.

Fairness of comparisons is debatable: baselines receive depth (DTArt) or per-part two-state captures, while DeGSS uses 4 multi-part states; input assumptions differ enough that the 'same 200-image budget' argument does not fully resolve protocol asymmetry, and the gains may partly reflect input format rather than the representation.
Generalization to unseen states is only demonstrated qualitatively (interpolation figures); no quantitative metric of interpolation/plausibility quality or collision/consistency check is provided.

Some technical components are derivative (SAGD-style splitting, standard Kabsch-based joint fitting, TSDF meshing), so the novelty rests mainly on the combination and the latent-conditioned deformation formulation; also minor issues such as undefined L_D_SIMM, incomplete derivation of the split-ratio 3D/2D equivalence, and typos ('inteactive', 'unmanual-prompt') suggest the manuscript would benefit from another pass.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and increasingly studied problem (multi-part, multi-state articulated object modeling) and the proposed pipeline is described in reasonable technical detail, including full method specifics in the appendix.

The experimental effort is substantial: an enlarged PartNet-Mobility split with multiple instances per category, a three-part harder subset, and a new real-to-sim benchmark (RS-Art) with digital-twin ground truth, which is a useful community resource.

Quantitative results on the synthetic benchmark are strong across axis, motion, and Chamfer metrics compared to PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, and ArtGS, and an ablation on the number of interaction states K is informative.

The coarse-to-fine segmentation idea (trajectory clustering + visibility-guided SAM prompting + boundary-aware Gaussian splitting) is a sensible mechanism and is supported by both qualitative and quantitative ablations.
weaknesses: The central claim of being 'fully self-supervised without human priors' is overstated and internally inconsistent. The method depends on a pre-trained VLM (InstructBLIP) to guess the number of parts, on SAM, and on multiple hand-tuned thresholds (τmot, τvis=1.2, the 2% cluster filter, the r<0.05 joint-type rule) that are never ablated. Baselines are criticized for needing the part count, yet the proposed method relies on an arguably stronger learned prior, just an implicit one.

The evaluation protocol is questionable: the authors report only the 'first run' for every method (Table 1) while admitting large run-to-run variance, and then argue that 'subsequent runs often produce even lower scores' for baselines without evidence. Mean±std over multiple seeds should be mandatory here; as presented, the comparison is not statistically trustworthy.

On the real-world RS-Art dataset, only ArtGS is compared against (all other baselines allegedly failed to converge), and the reported joint angle errors of ~0.3–1.5 degrees on real captures are suspiciously near-perfect; this weakens the realism claims considerably. The dataset itself is small (18 objects, green-screen chroma-key booth), limiting generality claims.

Novelty is limited: latent-conditioned deformation of Gaussian fields, trajectory-based clustering of primitives, and SAM-based Gaussian refinement are all established components; the contribution is largely their combination for articulated objects, and the positioning against DTArt/ArtGS could be sharpened rather than asserted.

Several technical claims are flawed or under-justified: the descriptor mixes unit directions with magnitudes and then applies ℓ2 normalization, so the assertion that 'Euclidean distance equals cosine distance on the unit sphere' does not hold for the actual feature vector; 'collision-free' extrapolation claims are asserted from qualitative figures only; generalization to unseen states is evaluated purely qualitatively.

Ablations are narrow: no ablation of the VLM-based part counting (e.g., how often is the mode wrong, how sensitive is clustering to a wrong nparts), of the motion descriptor design, of K-means vs. alternatives, or of τmot/τvis. Only the refinement stage and K are studied.

Writing and presentation have noticeable issues (e.g., 'inteactive state', 'unmanual-prompt', grammatical errors in Sec. 3.3, 'without refinement we... with of it'), and some notation inconsistencies (latent code α vs. z_k) reduce clarity. Text artifacts in Tables 2/3 ('F' entry for DTArt) are unexplained.
No code or data is available at review time despite claims of release, limiting reproducibility assessment.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: multi-part articulated object modeling without manual part counts or two-state assumptions, going beyond PARIS/ArticulatedGS/DTArt/ArtGS in scope.

The latent-conditioned deformation field over discrete interaction states is a sensible design that decouples each part's motion and enables interpolation to unseen configurations (Fig. 3), a capability baselines lack.

Comprehensive evaluation: expanded PartNet-Mobility split (2- and 3-part objects), joint-type/axis/motion and Chamfer metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablations on the refinement stage and on the number of states K (Tab. 5, Tab. 6), plus detailed appendix covering splitting, joint typing, and parameter estimation.

RS-Art is a useful community contribution: real RGB-D captures paired with reverse-engineered, physics-ready URDF/USD digital twins across 18 objects and 6 categories, well documented in the appendix.

The trajectory-based clustering plus visibility-guided SAM prompting and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting is a coherent coarse-to-fine segmentation pipeline, and the ablation quantifies its benefit (CD-m reduced ~60%).
weaknesses: The 'fully self-supervised' claim is overstated: the method depends on pretrained foundation models (SAM for mask prompting, InstructBLIP VLM for counting moved parts). Counting parts by querying a VLM with a fixed prompt is brittle, and no ablation quantifies the reliability of this VLM-based part-count estimation or its failure modes.

Evaluation protocol raises fairness and credibility concerns: baseline results are the 'first run' with acknowledged large run-to-run variance, and different methods receive different input configurations (baselines get 200 views per run with GT part counts; DTArt gets rendered depth; single-part methods are run per joint and merged). Reporting first-run numbers while claiming subsequent runs 'produce even lower scores' for baselines is not a rigorous protocol and could favor the proposed method. Mean errors (e.g., 0.33° axis angle) are dramatically better than all baselines and would benefit from variance reporting and statistical tests.

Comparison on RS-Art is thin: only ArtGS is compared quantitatively (Table 4), and the main-text real-data section shows essentially one qualitative example; the dataset's value as a benchmark would be strengthened by more baselines and more instances.

Novelty is moderate: latent-conditioned deformation of Gaussian primitives is close to existing dynamic/4D Gaussian splatting (Sec. 2 acknowledges this), and trajectory clustering + SAM-guided splitting composes known techniques (K-means, SAGD splitting); the contribution is primarily the system integration and the two-state-to-multi-state generalization.

Technical presentation has inconsistencies: the loss in Eq. (7) omits explicit regularization terms referenced in the text, latent symbols switch between z_k and α_k, Eq. (8) uses an undefined max_r, 'inteactive state' and other typos appear, and no standard rendering metrics (PSNR/SSIM) or runtime/memory costs are reported.

The RS-Art capture setup (chroma-key booth, single handheld RGB-D camera, ground truth built by caliper measurement and manual segmentation in Isaac Sim) limits the realism and precision of the 'real-to-sim' ground truth, and the claimed pixel-accurate digital twins are not validated quantitatively.

Assumes accurate camera poses across all states; sensitivity to pose noise is only mentioned as future work, and occlusion/textureless-surface failure modes (Sec. E) are acknowledged but not quantified.

strengths: Comprehensive problem formulation: models articulated objects as continuous deformations of a shared canonical 3DGS field with per-primitive latent-conditioned offsets, enabling multi-part, multi-state modeling beyond the common two-state/single-joint setups of prior work (PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, ArtGS).

Coarse-to-fine part segmentation is well motivated: trajectory-based clustering of Gaussian motion provides an unsupervised grouping signal, and the visibility-guided SAM prompting plus boundary-aware recursive Gaussian splitting (with quantitative ablations, e.g., 35% CD-s and 60% CD-m reductions) appears technically sound and well integrated into the 3DGS paradigm.

Extensive evaluation: enlarged PartNet-Mobility split with multiple instances per category, three- and five-part objects, a two-state fairness check (Tab. 3), unseen-state interpolation comparisons against dynamic NeRF/3DGS methods (Tab. 2), pose-noise robustness (Tab. 8), timing analysis (Tab. 10), and module-level ablations (Tabs. 11-15).

New RS-Art real-to-sim dataset (18 objects, 6 categories, 7 states, reverse-engineered 3D ground truth, URDF/USD assets) addresses a genuine gap in real-world evaluation for articulated object reconstruction and is a useful community resource.

Honest discussion of limitations (occlusion, screw joints, missing physical properties, accurate-pose assumption) and clear, detailed methodological exposition with appendix-level implementation details.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core components are largely assembled from existing techniques (deformable-3DGS-style latent-conditioned MLP deformation, K-means trajectory clustering, SAGD-style boundary-aware splitting, SAM prompting, VLM-based counting). The contribution is primarily a careful system integration rather than a fundamentally new representation or learning principle.

Several heuristics weaken robustness claims: VLM-based part-counting with a fixed prompt ('How many components moved?') is brittle and evaluated on only ~20 curated instances (100% accuracy is likely optimistic); the static/dynamic threshold τmot and visibility threshold τvis are tuned on representative instances; cluster noise merging (2%) and the revolute/prismatic rank rule (r<0.05) are hard-coded without sensitivity analysis.

Evaluation fairness concerns: single-part baselines consume 200×nparts images yet results are reported from 'the first run' with the claim that later runs are better for baselines — this framing invites skepticism; DTArt receives depth while others do not; baselines requiring known part counts get GT counts. Some asymmetries favor the proposed method despite the stated fairness protocol.

Real-world evidence is comparatively thin: RS-Art results are mostly qualitative (Fig. 7) with quantitative comparison only against ArtGS, which the authors say is the only baseline that runs reliably; no comparison to DTArt or other recent methods on real data, and only one quantitative table for 18 real objects.

Continuous control claims rest on interpolation between a small number of discrete latent codes (K=4-10); there is no analysis of how interpolations behave outside the convex hull of training states or for coupled/multi-joint simultaneous motion, so 'arbitrary interaction state' and 'fine-grained continuous control' claims are stronger than the evidence.

Table 1 shows the method is not uniformly superior (e.g., CD-w and CD-s are worse than DTArt on several categories, and ArtGS achieves very low axis-angle errors on some categories); the narrative of consistent superiority overstates the results.

Computational overhead is higher than the strongest baselines (35.6-44.8 min training vs. ArtGS's ~16-18 min), and the pipeline's dependence on foundation models (SAM, VLM) complicates reproducibility; code is only promised 'upon publication'.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: modeling interaction states as continuous deformations of a shared canonical Gaussian field addresses a genuine limitation of prior two-state / discrete-state articulated object methods (PARIS, DTArt, ArtGS), enabling latent-code interpolation to unseen configurations.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: expanded PartNet-Mobility split with 2-3 instances per category (addressing the one-instance-per-category weakness of prior work), objects with 2, 3, and 5 movable parts, comparison against single-joint, multi-joint, dynamic NeRF/GS, and generative baselines, plus timing analysis and camera-pose-noise robustness experiments.

A diverse set of ablations (refinement stage, number of interaction states K, VLM prompting strategies, SAM segmentation vs. SAGD, per-module analysis) that individually justify each pipeline component.
Release of RS-Art, a new real-to-sim RGB-D benchmark with reverse-engineered part-level ground truth, which is a valuable community resource for sim-to-real evaluation of articulated object modeling.
The method is fully self-supervised and requires no prespecified part count, unlike DTArt and ArtGS which require known part counts.
weaknesses: The pipeline is a long chain of heuristic, largely non-differentiable stages (VLM-based part counting with a fixed prompt, K-means trajectory clustering, visibility-aware SAM prompting, recursive boundary-aware splitting), each introducing hand-tuned thresholds (e.g., tau_mot, tau_vis tuned on 'one or two representative instances', the 2% cluster-merge rule, the rank-ratio 0.05 joint-type rule). This raises concerns about brittleness and potential dataset-specific tuning; sensitivity analyses for these thresholds are missing.

Reliance on a VLM queried with a fixed prompt ('Compare the two images. How many components moved?') is a fragile component; the claimed 100% count accuracy (Table 13) is on a small sample and may not generalize to ambiguous or visually similar parts.

Novelty is moderate: latent-conditioned deformation fields are well established in dynamic Gaussian splatting (4D-GS, Deformable-3DGS), and the segmentation components (SAM prompting, trajectory clustering, SAGD-style splitting) are largely borrowed; the contribution is primarily their composition and adaptation to the articulated-object setting.

Reporting the 'first run' for high-variance baselines, while justified as anti-cherry-picking, leaves some ambiguity about fairness; mean/median over multiple runs with variance bands would be more rigorous, especially given the very large margins in Table 1.

RS-Art ground truth comes from reverse-engineered digital twins; the fidelity of this annotation pipeline and its systematic error is not quantified, and the dataset size (18 objects, 6 categories) is modest.

The method assumes accurate camera poses and well-separated states, and the qualitative real-world results (Fig. 14) show noticeably degraded geometry under realistic lighting/textures, indicating the sim-to-real gap remains substantial.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: moving from discrete two-state pairwise matching to a shared canonical Gaussian field with latent-conditioned continuous deformation is a meaningful conceptual advance for articulated object modeling, and it enables capabilities (arbitrary number of states, unseen-state interpolation, multi-part control) that prior pipelines fundamentally lack.

Technically well-designed pipeline: the combination of motion-trajectory clustering for coarse part grouping, visibility-aware SAM prompting, and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting is a thoughtful integration, with the coarse-to-fine segmentation stage well justified by both the ablation (Fig. 8, Tab. 11) and the module-wise evaluation (Tab. 15).

Unusually thorough evaluation: multi-instance evaluation per category (2-3 instances across 8 categories, plus 3- and 5-part objects), matched image budgets across baselines (200 views), fair two-state protocol comparison (Tab. 3), robustness to camera pose noise (Tab. 8), runtime analysis (Tab. 10), and ablations on the number of interaction states K and VLM prompting strategies.

Strong empirical results: consistent and substantial improvements over PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, and ArtGS across joint-parameter and geometry metrics on both synthetic (Tab. 1, Tabs. 4-6) and real data (Tab. 7), plus superior unseen-state rendering versus deformable NeRF/3DGS baselines (Tab. 2).

Valuable community resource: the RS-Art real-to-sim dataset with reverse-engineered USD/URDF/PLY assets, part-level ground truth, and documented capture pipeline addresses a real gap in sim-to-real evaluation for this area, and the authors commit to releasing code and data.
Honest limitations section covering occlusion-related incompleteness, sparse-state ambiguity, and the absence of physical properties.
weaknesses: The pipeline is heuristic-heavy and brittle in places: multiple hand-tuned thresholds (τ_mot, τ_vis, 2% cluster-merge rule, rank-ratio 0.05 for joint typing), reliance on a VLM for part counting, and iterative SAM-guided splitting, all executed outside the optimization loop. Sensitivity of the full system to these choices is only partially analyzed (e.g., the reported 100% part-count accuracy in Tab. 13 appears optimistic and would benefit from testing on harder real-world categories).

Continuous deformation is achieved by interpolating per-state latent codes rather than learning an explicit kinematic model; quantitative validation of interpolated states is limited to rendering metrics against dynamic-scene baselines (Tab. 2), not against ground-truth intermediate geometry/kinematics, so the physical plausibility of in-between configurations is not rigorously verified.

The per-object optimization paradigm (canonical field + K latents trained per instance) means no cross-object generalization; the model must be retrained from scratch for every new object, which limits scalability relative to the digital-twin ambitions in the motivation.

Compared to recent dynamic 3DGS work, the core deformation mechanism (latent-conditioned per-primitive offsets) is an adaptation of existing ideas; the novelty lies mainly in the articulated-object-specific segmentation and supervision design rather than the deformation formulation itself.

Baselines operate under handicaps (single-joint pipelines run per part, two-state methods) that, while fairly budgeted, make some comparisons inherently unequal; DTArt's use of depth input is acknowledged but not fully controlled for.

Real-world evaluation on RS-Art is dominated by ArtGS because other baselines fail to converge; only one real-data baseline limits the strength of the sim-to-real claims, and the objects (green-screen booth, uniform lighting) are still a step below fully in-the-wild conditions.
